content: Adenomyosis is a condition characterized by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, the middle muscular layer of the uterine wall. This condition was first described as such, and the current definition, provided by Bird in 1972, describes it as a benign invasion of the endometrium into the myometrium, leading to a diffusely enlarged uterus. Microscopically, this condition exhibits ectopic, non-neoplastic endometrial glands and stroma surrounded by hypertrophic and hyperplastic myometrium. When the infiltration of endometrial glands forms grossly visible nodules without a capsule, distinct from the surrounding myometrium, it is referred to as adenomyoma. This condition is distinct from endometriosis, which involves the implantation of endometrial glands outside the uterus. Sampson's retrograde menstruation theory, proposed in the 1950s, suggested that menstrual cells entering the peritoneal cavity could implant and develop into endometriotic lesions, helping to differentiate endometriosis from adenomyosis. Adenomyosis is observed in approximately 30% to 60% of women undergoing hysterectomy. It is most commonly reported in women in their 40s and 50s, with 70% to 80% of cases occurring in this age group. However, between 5% and 25% of cases are observed in women younger than 39 years, and only 5% to 10% occur in women older than 60 years. While the diagnosis is typically made in symptomatic women in their 40s and 50s, it can also be found incidentally in younger women undergoing infertility evaluations or presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding and pain. Common symptoms of adenomyosis include menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding), dysmenorrhea (painful periods), metrorrhagia (irregular bleeding episodes), and dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse). The frequency and severity of these symptoms are related to the extent and depth of the adenomyotic lesions. Women with adenomyosis often have distinct symptomatology compared to those with leiomyomas (benign uterine tumors) and are more likely to experience depression, dysmenorrhea, and pelvic pain. Adenomyosis is more frequently observed in multiparous women, as pregnancy may facilitate the formation of adenomyosis by allowing adenomyotic foci to become embedded in the myometrium. Evidence regarding an increased risk of prior uterine surgery in women with adenomyosis is inconsistent. Hereditary occurrence has been reported, suggesting a genetic predisposition. Additionally, iatrogenic induction of the disease may result from endometrial ablation or trauma during endometrial resection. The pathogenesis of adenomyosis is thought to involve direct contact between the endometrial stroma and the underlying myometrium, allowing communication and interaction. Physical disruption of the endometrial-myometrial interface may result from dysfunctional uterine hyperperistalsis or sub-endometrial myometrial contractility dysfunction. The presence of estrogen, progesterone, and androgen receptors in adenomyotic tissue suggests that ectopic endometrium is hormone-dependent. Diagnostic advances have reduced the reliance on hysterectomy for histological confirmation of adenomyosis. Preoperative diagnosis can now be achieved using less invasive techniques such as ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Transvaginal ultrasonography is a cost-effective and feasible diagnostic option, although it is highly observer-dependent. MRI, particularly T2-weighted imaging, can identify the endo-myometrial junctional zone, with irregular thickening of this zone recognized as a hallmark of adenomyosis. Hormonal therapies for adenomyosis target the ectopic endometrium and aim to reduce its proliferation, decrease uterine volume, and alleviate symptoms such as abnormal bleeding and pain. Systemic hormonal therapy suppresses estrogenic stimulation of the disease by targeting the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, inducing a hypo-estrogenic state that regresses the lesions. Local hormonal therapy directly targets the ectopic endometrium, inducing atrophy of the endometrial glands and stromal decidualization. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists were among the first drugs used to treat adenomyosis. They act by down-regulating GnRH activity in the pituitary gland, creating a reversible state of medical menopause. This therapy reduces uterine volume, induces amenorrhea, and alleviates severe dysmenorrhea. However, discontinuation of therapy often leads to regrowth of the uterus and recurrence of symptoms. GnRH agonists are typically used for limited periods due to adverse effects such as hot flashes and decreased bone mineral density. The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (IUD) has been shown to induce endometrial gland atrophy and extensive stromal decidual transformation. It down-regulates estrogen receptors in the endometrium and has been effective in reducing menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea. Similarly, danazol-loaded IUDs have been found to induce remission of symptoms and allow spontaneous conception after removal. Aromatase inhibitors, which inhibit the enzyme aromatase P450 expressed in ectopic endometrium, have also been proposed as a treatment for adenomyosis. However, their use is associated with side effects such as joint and muscle pain, loss of bone density, osteoporosis, and hot flashes. Traditionally, hysterectomy has been the most common treatment for symptomatic adenomyosis. However, it is associated with perioperative and postoperative morbidity, decreased quality of life, and high healthcare costs. Non-invasive imaging techniques have enabled preoperative diagnosis, allowing for the exploration of less invasive treatment options. Hormonal therapy and minimally invasive surgical procedures, such as endometrial ablation, laparoscopic excision, and MRI-guided focused ultrasound, offer conservative management options for women wishing to preserve fertility.
